name: Computer Fundamentals and Applications
exam: TU assessment: 60% final examination set by the university, 40% internal (assignments, lab work, attendance). Confirm the split in your college's notice.

units.title: Introduction to Computer System
summary: A computer takes input, processes it under a stored program, stores data and produces output.
Computers are classified by size, purpose and the kind of data they handle; five generations are marked by tube, transistor, IC, microprocessor and ULSI/AI.
The CPU contains the ALU, control unit and registers; buses join CPU, memory and I/O.
Instructions and data share one memory in the von Neumann design; the CPU repeats fetch–decode–execute–store.
Memory is a hierarchy: speed and cost fall and capacity rises from registers to cache to RAM to disks and tape.
RAM is volatile and read–write; ROM is non-volatile and holds start-up firmware; flash is erasable ROM.
Input devices, output devices and interfaces (USB, HDMI, SATA, PCIe, wireless) connect the machine to the user.

units.title: Computer Software
summary: Software is divided into system software (OS, drivers, utilities, translators) and application software (general-purpose or custom).
Translators convert human-readable code to machine code; compilers do it once, interpreters do it each run.
Languages progress from machine code to assembly to high-level to declarative.
An algorithm is a finite, precise procedure; a flowchart draws it; sequence, selection and iteration are enough to express any algorithm.
Licences decide what you may do with software; open source gives freedoms, not freedom from conditions.

units.title: Operating System
topics: User interfaces and the boot process

sections.title: User interfaces and the boot process

summary: The OS manages processes, memory, files and devices and provides the user interface.
Multiprogramming keeps the CPU busy; time-sharing gives interactivity; real-time guarantees deadlines.
Scheduling algorithms trade fairness, throughput and waiting time; SJF is optimal for average wait but needs knowledge of burst lengths.
Paging maps pages to frames, virtual memory uses disk to extend RAM, and page faults cost time.
Files live in a directory tree on a file system; booting loads the kernel through firmware and a boot loader.

units.title: Database Management System
summary: A DBMS replaces scattered files with one controlled, shared and secure store.
The three-level architecture gives data independence.
Relational databases organise data into tables linked by keys, with integrity rules the DBMS enforces.
ER modelling designs the database; normalisation removes redundancy and anomalies.
SQL creates, queries and updates; transactions obey ACID.

units.title: Data Communication and Computer Network
topics: Advantages, limitations and uses of computer networks

sections.title: Advantages, limitations and uses of computer networks

summary: Communication needs a sender, receiver, message, medium and protocol; capacity is limited by bandwidth and noise.
Media may be guided (twisted pair, coax, fibre) or unguided (radio, microwave, satellite).
Networks are classified by scale (PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN) and by topology (bus, ring, star, mesh, tree).
Switches work on MAC addresses; routers on IP addresses; layered models (OSI, TCP/IP) divide the work.
IPv4 addresses split into network and host parts by a mask; subnetting divides a network into smaller ones.

units.title: Internet and the World Wide Web
topics: Names, addresses and the journey of a web page
Eight uses of the Internet in Nepal

sections.title: Names, addresses and the journey of a web page
Eight uses of the Internet in Nepal

summary: The Internet grew from ARPANET; the Web was added by Tim Berners-Lee around 1990.
DNS turns names into IP addresses; HTTP/HTTPS carries requests and responses over TCP.
Browsers render HTML, CSS and JavaScript; search engines crawl, index and rank.
Email, VoIP, streaming and cloud services all ride on the Internet.
Malware, phishing and weak passwords are the commonest threats; encryption, updates, 2FA and caution are the commonest defences.
Bandwidth sets how fast bulk data moves; distance sets the delay (a geostationary satellite adds about 0.48 s of round trip).
Nepal's main Internet uses: communication, education, payments, e-governance, e-commerce, health, maps and IoT.

units.title: Contemporary Technologies
topics: Virtual, augmented and mixed reality; robotics; 5G
Green computing, e-waste and cyber ethics

sections.title: Virtual, augmented and mixed reality; robotics; 5G
Green computing, e-waste and cyber ethics

summary: E-commerce and e-governance move trade and public service online; Nepali payment wallets and QR have made small payments digital.
Multimedia is digitised media; compression (lossless or lossy) makes it practical.
AI and ML learn from data; IoT collects data; big data and the cloud store and process it at scale.
Blockchain provides a tamper-evident shared ledger; VR/AR, robotics and 5G extend where computing reaches.
Every technology brings ethical and environmental responsibilities.

units.title: Laboratory Applications: Word Processor, Spreadsheet, Presentation and Photo Editing
summary: A word processor works best with styles, section settings and mail merge; macros automate but must be treated as a security risk.
A spreadsheet recalculates formulas, so it supports validation, protection, what-if analysis, consolidation and pivot tables.
A presentation supports a speaker: structure, master slides and restrained effects.
Bitmap graphics depend on resolution and colour depth; compression and format choice control file size.
